newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Adidas bets on more profit growth.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Adidas bets on more profit growth.

text.p: Adidas AG, reaping the benefits of major Olympic and soccer promotions last year, said on Tuesday its 1996 operating profit nearly doubled to 360 million marks ($211 million) as sales surged 35 percent to 4.71 billion marks.

Adidas, the sportswear maker known for its three-striped logo, said the sales and profit improvement was fuelled by internal growth from all areas of the world, including Europe where sales topped three billion marks for the first time.
North American sales rose 34 percent to 1.03 billion marks, with growth driven by running and training shoe sales and by basketball, replacing soccer as the strongest category.

Sales in the Asia-Pacific region grew the fastest within the group, surging 51 percent to 464 million marks due to the addition of sales from newly-formed joint ventures and subsidiaries in fast-growing markets.

Adidas said it was betting on further acceptance of its new shoe range called "Feet You Wear" which was introduced in the 1996 third quarter and has so far accounted for sales of about 600,000 pairs of shoes. Double-digit growth rates are expected for 1997, especially after new running shoes are introduced.
Adidas also said it planned to raise its 1996 dividend to 1.10 marks per share from 25 pfennigs in 1995, in part due to the 28 percent rise in net profit to 314 million marks.

"Adidas is geared to succeed in a highly competitive environment and we are committed to sustained growth in both sales and profits," Adidas chief executive Robert Louis-Dreyfus said at the company's annual news conference.

"Our business outlook is strong. The order backlog for 1997 is up substantially over last year's, at the same time demonstrating the tremendous acceptance of our brand and products by both the trade and consumers," he said.

Louis-Dreyfus said Adidas, which he helped to revive from the brink of bankruptcy in the early 1990s, would keep up the double-digit profit growth in the coming years but probably not at the same rate as in the last two years.
"I think the trend is that we will grow at double-digit rates, over 20 percent but not above 50 percent," he said in an interview after a company news conference in Frankfurt.

The higher sales and profit came after Adidas poured considerable funds into promotions for the Atlanta Olympics and the European soccer championships last summer as part of its total promotion budget pegged at 10 to 12 percent of sales.

Louis-Dreyfus said Adidas would step up spending in 1997 due to a fresh wave of high-profile endorsements, including the signing by Nike of golf star Tiger Woods to a five-year $40 million contract that he said "has changed the face of the industry".

Adidas, intent on breaking Nike's stranglehold on the lucrative North American sportswear market after an earlier attempt to break into the basketball market failed, responded by signing the New York Yankees baseball team to a reported 10-year, $95 million sponsorship deal.

Other sports teams signed to deals include the University of Notre Dame, one of the most high-profile college sports programmes in the United States, as well as individual stars such as Kobe Bryant of the Los Angeles Lakers basketball team.

"We are not focusing on Nike," Louis-Dreyfus said. "We are trying to do a good job with our product. But we think we need some key symbols and we think it will take higher advertising and promotion spending in America."
Louis-Dreyfus said Europe currently accounts for 57 percent of Adidas's global sales but he would like that level to fall to less than 50 percent by the turn of the century.
The goal was for North America to account for about 25 percent of worldwide sales in 2000 compared with around 22 percent now.
Louis-Dreyfus, who has said he would join the supervisory board in 1998, also sought to allay succession concerns, announcing five new members to the management board.
Adidas said the executives, which include chief financial officer Dean Hawkins and European sales manager Herbert Hainer, have held senior positions within Adidas for several years.
--Frankfurt Newsroom, +49 69 756525 ($ = 1.705 German Marks)
